STRENGTHS

Framing and structure. Brandon consistently led with a brief theoretical framing before diving into specifics, making it immediately clear he understood what was being asked before answering it. It made every answer feel precise and grounded, and never once felt like stalling.

People development instincts. He was the first interviewee to actually articulate the distinct growth dimensions for a TPM (program sense, business acumen, leadership influence, and technical depth) and used that framework to structure his coaching example. The instincts are clearly there even without formal management experience.

Product and engineering fluency. Brandon spoke intelligently about the product/eng dynamic: PMs tend to want to test and iterate broadly, while engineers prefer a narrower scope they can execute well. His approach, working with product to prioritize asks so the team could still explore a few high-conviction options, showed real maturity in navigating that tension without flattening it.

AI perspective. His framing, that the bottleneck for development is shifting away from engineers, and that anyone can build now, including TPMs, was sharp and original. He backed it up with a compelling example: building a tool that allowed customers to troubleshoot issues with AI assistance before being routed to a support agent, saving significant time on customer support calls. Practical, specific, and differentiated.


THINGS TO NOTE

No formal people management experience. Brandon has never been a direct people manager, which is worth flagging. That said, he was a founding member of the TPM mentorship community at Block and gave compelling examples of developing peers. The instincts seem strong here, even if the formal experience isn't there yet.

Most recent role is internal/operational. His recent work has been less direct-to-consumer. He does have D2C experience earlier in his background, and we should encourage him to lean on those examples in future rounds with the team.

Worth considering for the D&A/CBS role. If Brandon turns out not to be the right fit for the Premium TPM role, he'd be a strong candidate for the D&A/CBS opening. His data-focused approach and systems thinking feel well-suited for that context.

values.ef797525-33f7-4163-b509-86c8454b31e7:
Strengths

Managing through chaos. A compelling example. She joined Block mid-stride and Covid created an immediate crisis: an e-commerce feature for online selling that was going to take four months needed to ship in two weeks, with sellers suddenly dependent on pickup and delivery. Lauren was clearly operating across both product and engineering, surfacing risks, managing dependencies, and keeping the focus on business priorities rather than just operational ones. Exactly the kind of example we're looking for.

Product and engineering partnership. She spoke fluently about the natural tension between product optimizing for time to market and engineering optimizing for the right technical solution. Her specific example (identifying the biggest launch risk as too much parallel eng work creating broken flows, and rallying the team around business outcomes and user experience to create a sense of shared purpose) showed real cross-functional instinct and maturity.

People development. A nuanced coaching example. Her TPM had been set up to fail, dropped into a team that had never worked with a TPM, saddled with unrealistic expectations around owning the full project portfolio and doing heavy admin work. But Lauren also identified what the TPM themselves needed to change: being more vocal, operating from a strategic driver POV rather than a reactive one. She got to the root cause, moved them to a better-suited part of the org, and saw a remarkable turnaround. The combination of systemic diagnosis and individual coaching is the right instinct.

AI and the future of the role. Strong answer: spoke to automating repetitive work to free up judgment, and backed it up with a concrete example of building a summary dashboard for ongoing programs.

Flags to Address

Process simplification example missed the mark. She started well, describing a burdensome annual planning process that created false precision and wasted effort. But rather than describing how she removed or simplified it herself, the story turned into: the leader who created the process left, the company removed it, chaos ensued, and Lauren added a new lightweight quarterly planning cadence. Everything in the example made sense, but it's not actually an example of Lauren proactively simplifying or removing process: it's an example of her adding process back after someone else removed it. We should encourage her to find an example where she was the one to cut overhead, or where she enabled a more flexible and adaptive approach in partnership with other teams. In our role, showing that we don't just add overhead but can actively remove it is an important signal.

Management approach had limits. Defaulting to moving her TPM to a better-suited team worked in context, but that option won't always exist. Sometimes you have to make it work with the stakeholders you have, and it would be good to hear examples of that. One other note: her framing of a good TPM goal as "this program would fall apart without you" is worth gently pushing back on. That's a single point of failure, not a success. Our goal should be to make programs organized enough that they can run without us, so we can hand them off and move to the next most complex challenge.

Summary

Lauren is a strong candidate with real range: strategic, execution-oriented, and good with people. The flags are there but addressable. Excited to see her in the panel round.

values.b110f169-da06-4d91-9eaf-e538807729ae:
Lauren's strongest GRIT examples were the Square R&D governance redesign, the printer-reliability OKR tiger-team intervention, and the absorbed TPM she coached through a reorg.

On the R&D governance, two executives came to her with a narrow ask for a shared planning tool after Block functionalized from 20 GM-led product groups into one engineering, product, and design org; she expanded the ask into a full tool-and-process change, moved the company from annual to quarterly planning, drafted exec-fronted communication so the org would read it as a leadership change rather than a TPM push, and invested in trainings and office hours to keep engineers' day-to-day workflow undisrupted.

On the printer-reliability OKR, she noticed flat progress despite multi-team effort, used the monthly OKR review forum to reframe the conversation away from default-resolve hope toward a structural tiger-team intervention, and the resulting conversation surfaced a different solution than the default path.

On the absorbed TPM, she diagnosed the specific gap (strong PM craft, no engineering confidence), built a three-prong coaching approach (shadowing senior TPMs, reframing the role toward active technical engagement, targeted self-learning), and progressively scaled the difficulty of the mentee's programs from low-risk starters to more complex work, culminating in the mentee finding her career path and landing a TPM offer in an engineering-focused role at another company.
values.6e78c927-1f76-4b5d-82d1-c3e7c7611d99:
My focus was on Eng Strategy & Execution, specifically: (1) higher-level vision and strategy, (2) bubbling project-level signal into an exec-level program health view, (3) anticipating Eng-org needs at the 1+ year horizon, (4) being a thought partner to Eng leaders, and (5) management.

Evaluation Rubric: Each scenario-based question below was evaluated using a Red, Yellow, Green rubric:

 1. Green: Strong signal. Concrete example with named context, clear ownership, explicit tradeoffs, and evolution or learning. Strategic opinion shows up, not just process.

 2. Yellow: Acceptable but incomplete signal. Sound instincts or frameworks, but thin on specifics, or answered a nearby question rather than the one asked. Viewed as developmental rather than risky.

 3. Red: Concerning signal. Abstract, deflects ownership, minimizes impact, or cannot produce a real example.


QUESTION 1: OPERATING MODEL DESIGN UNDER STRATEGY

"At Block you architected Square's global R&D governance aligning $1B+ in annual investment across 1,500 engineers to business OKRs, and separately you developed the Block Engineering TPM Career Ladder across the company for 50+ TPMs. Pick whichever example you want and walk me through the decision: what was the situation that made this shape of program the right answer at that moment, how you arrived at it, and a year or two in, what did you know coming out the other side that you did not know going in?"

Result: Green

She picked the R&D governance work and grounded the diagnosis in a specific corporate moment. Block had operated as an "ecosystem of startups" with 20 different GM-led product groups, each with its own resourcing and P&L. Two years ago the company functionalized: merged the 20 groups into one engineering, product, and design org. The functionalization broke the implicit coordination model, and two executives came to her with a narrow ask (a shared planning tool to house all the roadmaps). Her strategic move was to expand the ask: just implementing a tool was not going to be enough, what they needed was a planning process around it. She moved the company from an annual to a quarterly planning cadence (her judgment was that 11-month-out predictions were no longer landing well as the industry accelerated). She launched the tool and process together, drafted exec-fronted communication so the org would not read it as a TPM-pushed change, and invested heavily in change management (trainings, office hours, Slack channels, FAQ) to keep engineers' day-to-day workflow undisrupted. Her retrospective: implementing process at scale requires repositioning your mental model from small-org buy-in to large-org change management, and accepting that you will not make everyone happy.

Key positives:

 - Specific company-moment diagnosis (functionalization from 20 GM-led groups to one org broke the coordination model)

 - Real strategic-design choice (expand the tool ask into a tool-plus-process change, move to quarterly cadence, exec-fronted comms, change-management investment)

 - Explicit retrospective with a real lesson (mental-model shift required for large-org change vs small-org familiarity)

 - Creator-pattern work throughout (she expanded the scope, chose the cadence, designed the comms approach)

What was less concrete:

 - The "what alternatives did you consider and reject" dimension was light. Why quarterly specifically (vs half-yearly), why this tool (vs others), and what she deliberately deprioritized did not surface explicitly.

 - The retrospective leaned defensive at the close ("there are just going to be naysayers, that is part of the process"). That is true, but it is a different shape from a specific lesson she would apply differently next time.

The strongest Q1 of the loop. Creator-level operating-model work at $1B+ scale with a clear diagnosis, named design choices, and a real retrospective. Adrian's Q1 was Yellow with Green elements; Ariela's was Yellow with the Fox-adaptation transparency; Lauren's is full Green.


QUESTION 2: EXEC-LEVEL ROLLUP, TRANSLATING PROJECT SIGNAL

"Your resume describes designing and facilitating Product Execution Reviews, OKR Reviews, and Reliability Reviews at Square, establishing executive-level visibility into system health and goal tracking. Give me a concrete example of a program where a skip-level or exec was about to draw the wrong conclusion because of how status was being rolled up to them. What was the information gap, what did you change about the rollup, and what is now non-negotiable in how you report program health up?"

Result: Yellow leaning Green

She told the printer-reliability OKR story. Square serves restaurants, and back-of-house networking issues kept stalling order receipts from printing. The OKR was being tracked monthly, and the numbers were not moving. Leadership's implicit conclusion was that the existing org structure would resolve it as long as it stayed listed and tracked as an OKR. Lauren caught the pattern (flat progress despite people across multiple teams working on it) and used the OKR review forum to reframe the conversation: do we need to look at this structurally rather than expecting it to resolve itself? She proposed a tiger team (small team dedicated for a defined period, accepting that resources would have to come from other parts of the business). Product and others chimed in once the structural question was on the table (the competitive context around Toast as a restaurant-tech threat became part of the conversation), and the team landed on a different solution than the default-resolve path.

Key positives:

 - Real named example with specific technical context (back-of-house printer reliability, networking issues, restaurant context)

 - Caught a default-optimism pattern in the rollup (exec implicit conclusion that the existing structure would resolve the OKR)

 - Used the exec review forum as a catalyst for structural rethinking rather than as a status read-out

 - Real outcome (the conversation sparked led to a different solution)

What was less concrete:

 - The shape is adjacent to the question. The failure mode was less about a misleading rollup and more about exec implicit hope that tracking alone would resolve a stalled OKR. Lauren caught that hope and reframed it, which is real exec-comms judgment, but it is a different shape from Adrian's CFO Nelson story or Ariela's Motion Canvas value-units rebuild.

 - The "what is now non-negotiable in how you report program health up" dimension was not directly answered. The implicit non-negotiable (use OKR forums to prompt structural rethinking when progress is flat) is there but unstated.

Real exec-comms judgment with a clean structural-intervention move. Yellow leaning Green because the question's failure-mode-rollup framing landed sideways rather than dead-center.


QUESTION 3: BEING A THOUGHT PARTNER TO ENG, 1+ YEAR HORIZON

"Tell me about a time you saw a structural need in the engineering org 6 to 12 months before anyone else was flagging it. Maybe a capability gap, a platform risk, a team-shape problem, an org-design issue. How did you form the view, what did you propose, and how did the eng leadership receive it?"

Result: Green

She gave two examples that both hit the foresight dimension. The larger-scale one was an org-design call: Square's roadmap was product-dictated, and from conversations with engineers (including ICs, not just senior leadership) she developed the view that tech debt was accumulating because engineering-driven initiatives could not bubble up through the existing planning process. As she was designing the new quarterly planning process she brought this to the head of product and won an allocation in the roadmap for engineering-driven initiatives (tech debt, performance, reliability) that previously had no path. The smaller-scale one was an architecture-risk call: working on Square's international expansion into Ireland, France, and Spain, she identified the hard-coded address form as a refactor candidate, explicitly framed against a 6-to-12-month horizon (would the team accumulate more tech debt on the highest-revenue surface of the product if they expanded into new markets without refactoring first), and made the call with the tech lead to refactor before expanding rather than after.

Key positives:

 - Two examples, both hitting the foresight dimension. The larger one is an org-design call (roadmap-process gap), the smaller one is a platform-risk call (architecture refactor before international expansion)

 - The smaller example explicitly named the "6 to 12 months from now" timeframe in her own words

 - Both forms-of-view came from her vantage point (engineer conversations for the larger; tech-lead conversation for the smaller) rather than being handed to her

 - Both produced real outcomes (engineering-driven roadmap allocation; pre-expansion refactor)

What was less concrete:

 - The "how did eng leadership receive it" dimension was light on the larger example (agreement was reached but pushback dynamics were not described)

 - The "have you been wrong about one of these" probe was not asked, so the humility-and-learning dimension is unverified

Comparable to Adrian's platform-team CTO escalation and Ariela's Volumetric Capture hiring-constraint story. Green-band Q3 with two examples, which is more than any other candidate provided.


QUESTION 4: PLAYER/COACH DEPTH

"You managed 10 TPMs at L5-L7 levels at Block and you built the Block Engineering TPM Career Ladder across the company for 50+ TPMs. Pick one specific TPM you hired or coached who grew significantly under you. Walk me through what you did, what you learned about your own coaching style, and how you think about the difference between managing engineers and managing a TPM team. Then tell me how the experience of building the Career Ladder changed how you coach individual TPMs day-to-day."

Result: Green

She told the story of a TPM she absorbed during a reorg. The TPM had a strong program management background but had not worked closely with engineering before; the reorg put her in that position for the first time. Lauren's read of the gap was specific (strong PM craft, hardworking, good communicator, but no engineering confidence). Her response had three explicit prongs: (1) shadowing senior TPMs in engineering meetings to absorb how they navigated technical conversations, (2) reframing the role away from "schedule meetings and take notes" toward active engagement (helping make tradeoffs, surfacing risks engineers might see but not voice), and (3) targeted self-learning via trainings. She also scaffolded the work: started the mentee with smaller, lower-risk programs to build confidence, then progressively expanded scope. Outcome: the mentee just got a TPM offer at another company in an engineering-focused role, and told Lauren she had found her career path.

Key positives:

 - Named mentee with named career outcome (offer at another company in an engineering-focused TPM role)

 - Specific three-prong coaching approach with rationale for each prong

 - Explicit reframing of the role away from logistics toward active technical engagement

 - Scaffolded difficulty progression as a deliberate coaching choice

What was less concrete:

 - The engineer-vs-TPM management distinction in the question was not directly addressed. The mentee was a PM transitioning into TPM work, not the engineer-management dimension specifically.

 - The "how did building the Career Ladder change how you coach individual TPMs day-to-day" probe was not directly answered. The mentee story stood alone rather than connecting to the systemic work.

Real coaching depth with a named mentee outcome. Tied with Ariela's Backup A for the strongest player/coach demonstration of the loop, though Ariela explicitly addressed the engineer-vs-TPM framework while Lauren addressed PM-to-TPM transition.


ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS

Her intro was clean and well-structured, hitting the relevant arc. Time-and-coverage management was strong throughout: she stayed within reasonable depth on each answer and did not run long the way some prior candidates did. Her examples were drawn from real situations she had lived; whether each example was comprehensive against the specific question dimensions was a different matter, but the underlying experience was real.

The candidate-question segment was the strongest in-room moment for the TPM-craft dimension. After her first question and my answer, she took what I said and reflected it back in TPM-lens at a high level, teasing apart the bottlenecks and problematic areas I had described. That kind of real-time synthesis of an engineering leader's strategic concerns into TPM-craft problems she would own is exactly the work a Senior Manager TPM does at this level, and she did it unprompted in a single conversational beat.

She came across as confident, professional, and mature. I could see myself working with her and her working well with the rest of my team, which is the strongest in-room fit signal I have flagged for any candidate in this loop.

Soft body-language observation worth noting and not over-reading: she appeared slightly deeper in thought before answering Q2 than before Q1, and moved into Q3 with visible eagerness. The pattern is consistent with the per-question rubric (Q2 landed sideways from the question center, Q3 landed cleanly), so the body language and the substance corroborate each other.

The implementer-vs-creator probe lands clearly on the creator side. Across her answers she described decisions she made, design choices she expanded, and structural moves she initiated, rather than describing processes she found and operated within. The "we" framing showed up but less heavily than in Adrian, Deep, or Jared. She was more comfortable saying "what I did was..." and "I made sure to..." than the average candidate in this loop, which made the individual ownership of design choices easier to read.

One concern worth flagging that I did not have time to probe directly. Lauren is coming from much bigger companies (Block/Square at $1B+ R&D scope across 1,500-engineer orgs), and Scribd is materially scrappier by design. We move fast, pivot, roll up sleeves as needed, and that hands-on energy is part of the engineering DNA here. Her most recent role at Block was leading 10 TPMs, which is closer to pure-manager scope than to the player/coach shape this role calls for. Her demeanor in the room was calm, stoic, and professional throughout, and none of her answers surfaced a moment of getting into the thick of things at the hands-on level. Every story she told operated at the strategic, structural, or coaching level rather than at the IC-execution level. This is partly intuition and could be over-reading a stoic communication style, but worth flagging because the player half of the player/coach framing is the half that is least obvious from her resume and least probed in my interview.

values.feedback: This was just a prep call, but Lauren handled it well and asked all the right questions.

values.3d8f2226-5da1-4831-93d8-ce15d6cf6994:
Overall Impression

Lauren remains one of the strongest candidates we've seen from a structural and organizational standpoint. But flexibility and proactiveness are critical attributes for a TPM at Scribd, and the final round made clear she doesn't fully have it. Regretfully, a no.

What Held Up

The presentation was organized, well-prepared, and easy to follow. Lauren clearly put in real work.

Where It Fell Short

The same core issue as her earlier rounds, amplified. The presentation followed a very classic, rigorous program structure from initiation to conclusion: well-executed, but without a distinct or original take. What was notably absent was any meaningful discussion of where she adapted, where she pulled back structure, or where she proactively shaped the direction of the program rather than responding to external inputs. This is exactly what I flagged directly with Lauren in a conversation ahead of the presentation: I was as specific and directive as I could be about the importance of showing flexibility and proactive shaping. She acknowledged it as good feedback. And then the presentation didn't reflect it. That gap is hard to explain away, and tells me she may not have truly operated this way in her previous roles, not just that she didn't communicate it well.

The AI slide was surprisingly thin. Given how much Lauren had spoken about working with AI, the "now with AI" slide at the end was underwhelming; basic ideas like summarizing reporting, alongside suggestions that were clearly out of scope for a TPM (like finding and addressing bugs, which sits with engineering). It didn't match the fluency she had implied earlier.

Q&A solidified the concern. Lauren frequently referred back to the presentation rather than adding new thinking, and her answers felt defensive at times. The most telling moment was her response to Aroash's question on escalations. Aroash was likely probing for Lauren's proactiveness in surfacing issues and exercising judgment. Instead, Lauren interpreted the question as concern that she might be making too much noise, and oriented her answer around avoiding bothering leadership. When asked a follow-up (whether she wished she had escalated anything) she said no, and framed solving problems independently as a point of pride. That's the wrong instinct. Escalation, done well and at the right moment, is a tool, not a failure. The fact that she doesn't seem to see it that way is a meaningful flag.

Summary

Lauren is genuinely strong on structure and organization. But the final round confirmed what earlier rounds hinted at: flexibility, proactive shaping, and knowing when to deviate from the plan aren't fully in her toolkit. For this role, that matters too much to overlook.

values.ef797525-33f7-4163-b509-86c8454b31e7:
Sheldon – Interview Feedback

Overall Impression

Smart, well-prepared candidate with good TPM instincts, but operating at a level below what this role requires. Not the right fit for the Senior Manager position, though worth keeping in mind for the CBS/D&A TPM role.

Strengths

Sheldon interviewed well. Responses were structured, time-bound, and always on topic: never rambled, never went long. He came prepared with good questions and a clear understanding of the role. He also came across as genuinely passionate about the TPM craft, with the sense that he's reflected on it beyond his day-to-day, which is an appealing quality.

Within his program experience, he demonstrated solid collaboration instincts: a good example of driving buy-in between product and engineering on mobile feature prioritization showed real judgment and cross-functional maturity.

Where He Fell Short

Depth over breadth. The bulk of Sheldon's recent experience seems to be centered on a single program: launching FanDuel in a specific Canadian province. He has accumulated good instincts within that context, but this role requires someone managing a portfolio of programs and building process and systems across a wide area of ownership. That's a different operating model, and it wasn't evident he's worked at that level.

No formal management experience. He has coached more junior TPMs, and the examples he shared showed good judgment, particularly around helping early-career TPMs evolve from being glorified assistants to driving real value. But the seniority gap between who he's coached and who he'd be managing at Scribd is significant.

Overall operating level. The cumulative impression was of a strong senior TPM rather than a senior manager. The skills are real, but they're calibrated to a different scope.

Recommendation

Don't move forward on this role, but be explicit with Sheldon that this is a scope and role/level mismatch, not a reflection of his ability. He could be a strong fit for the CBS/D&A TPM role (P4), and we should let him know we may reach out for that if he's open to it.

values.ef797525-33f7-4163-b509-86c8454b31e7:
Overall Impression

One of the best candidates we've seen for this role. Rare combination of structure, natural delivery, and genuine strategic depth. Strong yes, and given where we are in the process with Lauren, I'd recommend skipping the Emily round and moving straight to a panel, ideally scheduled for Monday.

Strengths

Presence and delivery. Anna was structured and organized throughout, but never once felt like she was reading from prepared remarks. Answers were crisp and to the point: never rambled, never padded. That combination of polish and naturalness has been quite rare throughout the process.

Across-the-board strength. She gave strong answers on every dimension: organizing chaos, influencing stakeholders, building bridges between parties with seemingly mutually exclusive goals, simplifying and removing process, coaching underperformers, and the evolving role of TPM in an AI world. What struck me was how instantly she could connect each question to what it meant from the perspective of a TPM leader, and produce a lived, specific example that made clear she'd thought through the issue before.

The process simplification example was the standout. This is the area where TPMs most commonly struggle, and Anna's answer was the strongest we've heard on it. She inherited a Voice of Customer program that had become enormously burdensome: teams doing manual work to surface large volumes of customer feedback in a way that overwhelmed executives without driving real decisions. She rebuilt it from the ground up: brought in AI tooling to distill and deduplicate feedback, compressed the output to 5-10 monthly trends with a clear yes/no/maybe framing on whether to act, and reduced exec touchpoints to a monthly business review. In the process, she surfaced a $25k per day issue with Stripe wallet. That's the kind of proactive, strategic thinking this role needs.

Recommended Guidance Before the Panel

Beyond the standard overview of who she'll be speaking with and what they're focused on, emphasize two things: proactiveness, and a willingness to deviate from formal structure and adapt when the situation calls for it. Those are some of the qualities the panel will be looking for that most candidates stumble over, and Anna should come ready to speak to them directly.
